title: Evaluate‑and‑Repair for LLM‑Generated NetOps Changes: A Preregistered Generate–Verify–Repair Study with a Deterministic Net Verifier
abstract: We report a fully preregistered, within‑task paired experiment (N=300 canonical device‑change tasks: routing 150 / ACL 100 / BGP 50) that measured whether a Generate–Verify–Repair (GVR) pipeline—an LLM proposer (gpt‑5‑mini) whose proposals are gated by a deterministic network verifier and, on rejection, given one automated repair iteration—reduces the acceptance of proposals that would create unsafe or policy‑violating sandbox states versus LLM‑only proposals. Design (frozen): paired binary outcome per task = verifier‑anchored "would‑cause‑unsafe‑state‑if‑applied"; primary test = McNemar exact two‑sided; bootstrap 95% CI (10k, seed=1729). Results: complete pairs = 300; baseline unsafe = 1/300 (0.3333%); guarded (GVR) unsafe = 0/300 (0.00%); paired absolute reduction = 0.003333 (0.3333 percentage points); McNemar p = 1.00; bootstrap 95% CI = [0.00, 0.01]. The single baseline unsafe case (task‑000165) was corrected by the automated repair iteration; raw proposer outputs, verifier counterexamples, repair call JSONs and full provenance are archived (execution_manifest and analysis artifact hashes cited in the Disclosure). We present methods, exact verifier checks, the representative repair episode, limitations, and the reproducibility recipe required for deterministic replay.

sections.introduction: Generative LLMs can convert operator intent into device configuration proposals, but stochastic generation risks producing changes that are syntactically plausible yet operationally unsafe (e.g., unintended reachability, ACL weakening, or non‑reversible control‑plane edits). Operational NetOps requires deterministic acceptance decisions and auditable traces. The Generate–Verify–Repair (GVR) pattern interposes deterministic verifiers between probabilistic generation and acceptance and uses repair context to iteratively refine proposals. Prior surveys and single‑case studies motivate verifier‑anchored workflows, but there is a gap for preregistered, deterministically archived, within‑task experiments that measure whether a verifier gate plus short repair loop reduces verifier‑detectable unsafe proposals relative to LLM‑only generation. We therefore preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory study (CNSM2026‑GVR‑BATFISH‑CAND‑001) to quantify verifier gating + 1 repair iteration effects on verifier‑visible hazards in a canonical NetOps sandbox.
sections.related_work: This study brings together three strands. (1) GVR and verifier‑anchored architectures for converting stochastic generation into verifier‑acceptable artifacts (Cadenas 2026 formalizes GVR for compliance‑critical code; Gao et al., RAG survey, arXiv:2312.10997). (2) Network configuration verification literature (Header Space Analysis, SymNet/SEFL, and iptables static verification) that informs deterministic reachability and policy checks (SymNet: DOI 10.1145/2934872.2934881; formal reachability & update verification: Li et al., COMNET 2020 DOI 10.1016/j.comnet.2020.107326). (3) Agentic NetOps/AIOps surveys arguing for assurance contracts, bounded tool use and verifier gates (Bilal et al., arXiv:2605.12729). Our contribution differs: a frozen preregistered paired protocol, deterministic verifier decision rules archived prior to model calls, and a complete provenance bundle enabling deterministic replay.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and frozen design. The study preregistration (CNSM2026‑GVR‑BATFISH‑CAND‑001; SHA‑256: 156e87e6ce4a9a2348525fa8960f35fb4120031344cf4b4a38b247b10893181b) froze: task sampling (seed 2026‑08‑25), proposer model (gpt‑5‑mini), verifier checks/thresholds, repair budget (≤1 automated repair invocation), estimands, primary analysis (McNemar exact two‑sided), bootstrap CI plan, missingness/exclusion rules and stopping rules. Task bank and sampling. Deterministic stratified sampling produced 300 canonical device tasks: routing 150, ACL 100, BGP 50. Proposer and orchestration. Proposer = gpt‑5‑mini (hosted API); adapter = hosted_netops_gvr_v1; all provider calls, raw outputs and model‑call JSONs archived (execution_manifest). Deterministic verifier (frozen and archived). The primary binary outcome per task is the verifier judgment "would‑cause‑unsafe‑state‑if‑applied". The frozen verifier implements these checks (implementation and decision rules archived at execution/transformation_manifest.json; SHA‑256: f3ac546043ac61cb7222b01c975a3cb98d8f309bb7f65f636ab98667e98608b5): 1) Reachability regression: header‑space style comparison that detects newly permitted flows violating canonical reachability policy anchors (i.e., flows previously denied that would become permitted). 2) ACL/policy flip: detection of policy rule transitions from DENY→ALLOW for flows marked protected in the frozen policy matrix. 3) Parse/semantic invalidity: proposals that cannot be parsed into the canonical device representation or that contain semantically inconsistent constructs (treated as unsafe). 4) Deterministic safety predicates: removal of mandated connectivity or introduction of non‑reversible control‑plane edits per a frozen safety predicate list. These predicates were fixed and archived before any model calls. Guarded flow and repair loop (frozen). Guarded (GVR) flow: proposer→verifier; on verifier rejection the verifier returns a structured counterexample (packet tuple + violating rule); proposer is re‑invoked once with repair context (repair budget = 1). All raw proposer outputs, parsed canonical patches, verifier traces and repair provider calls were logged and archived. Statistical analysis (frozen). Primary test: McNemar exact two‑sided on paired binary outcomes. Report absolute and relative reductions and exact p. Paired bootstrap (10,000 resamples, seed=1729) yields a 95% percentile CI for the paired absolute difference. Exclusions and missingness. Preplanned deterministic exclusion rules applied: generation failures (no parseable config) would be recorded as model failure and excluded for that arm only; paired tests use only complete pairs. No episodes were excluded in the executed run. Reproducibility recipe. Minimal files needed to reproduce primary table/figure: execution/raw_results.jsonl (SHA‑256: 68c8168fff763b5530f4b36681a8956f5bbfb4ff98f6753a12cae97b017ee8e1), execution/transformation_manifest.json (verifier rules; SHA‑256: f3ac5460...), execution/model_configuration.json (a40e96e2...), execution/task_manifest.jsonl (7df39740...), analysis scripts and analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv (3421adb5...). All paths and SHA‑256 values appear in the execution_manifest.
sections.results: Execution provenance and counts. Run completed 2026‑08‑25; planned episodes = 600; completed = 600; model calls used = 301 (300 initial + 1 repair). Confirmatory 2×2 counts (paired): safe both = 299; unsafe baseline only = 1; unsafe guarded only = 0; unsafe both = 0. Observed rates and inferential results (units stated consistently as proportions and percentages): baseline unsafe = 1/300 = 0.003333 (0.3333%); guarded unsafe = 0/300 = 0.000000 (0.00%). Paired absolute reduction = 0.003333 (0.3333 percentage points). McNemar exact two‑sided p = 1.00 (discordant counts b=1, c=0). Paired bootstrap (10,000 resamples, seed=1729) 95% percentile CI for absolute reduction = [0.00, 0.01] (i.e., [0.0%, 1.0%]). Task‑type breakdown (observed unsafe proposals): routing (150): baseline 0, guarded 0; ACL (100): baseline 1, guarded 0; BGP (50): baseline 0, guarded 0. Representative repaired episode (artifact‑grounded). Task ID: task‑000165. Archived artifacts and SHA‑256s: execution/responses/task-000165-baseline.txt = 4c4df2ec851732cd7a6302211bbc79b5099a1bf6d470204b6ac883446bcd09f2; execution/responses/task-000165-guarded.txt = b4faabeaaf3bd9e0fae78adc1bbb3b40ff36d95e95ac6796c2f0000c2af2b8ff; execution/provider_calls/task-000165-guarded-repair.json = 93d0712d93248452202c8a1f0051ca4a619a1c835a9af1f828494aed1f033ebc. Sequence (archival excerpts): (A) Baseline proposer produced an ACL patch that the verifier flagged because a canonical protected flow (src:10.0.0.0/24 → dst:172.16.0.0/12, TCP/22) became permitted; verifier counterexample recorded the offending rule and packet tuple. (B) The single repair invocation used that counterexample as repair context; proposer returned an amended ACL patch that passed the verifier. Full raw texts and verifier traces for this episode are archived at the listed paths for deterministic audit and replay (see Disclosure manifest). Analysis artifacts. Paired contingency table and analysis scripts are archived (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv SHA‑256: 3421adb52d5791a979397368165fc2062e6b9a4a771ce49c0bcac80b02215d55; analysis log SHA‑256: a509c04a5f75eee720ad01e443807b72d1c670a43b964cfb2b4fe5b45db740d5).
sections.discussion: Interpretation. In this canonical sandbox, a deterministic verifier gate plus one automated repair iteration corrected the only verifier‑detectable unsafe baseline proposal (task‑000165) and produced deterministic acceptance traces. Mechanistically, GVR converted a stochastic, unsafe proposer output into a verifier‑acceptable artifact while emitting an auditable counterexample and a repair trace. Statistical caveat. The observed baseline hazard rate is very low (1/300), which limits inferential sensitivity for modest absolute improvements: McNemar p=1.00 and bootstrap CI [0.00,0.01] reflect that low event count. Construct validity and verifier scope (explicit). The primary outcome measures verifier‑visible hazards, not comprehensive production safety. The frozen verifier (execution/transformation_manifest.json; SHA‑256: f3ac5460...) implements reachability regression (header‑space style) checks, ACL/policy‑flip detection for protected flows, parse/semantic validity checking against the canonical device model, and deterministic safety predicates that detect mandated‑connectivity removals or non‑reversible control‑plane edits. Intentionally out‑of‑scope verifier areas (also preregistered) include vendor‑specific dynamic control‑plane subtleties, timing/race conditions in multi‑change promotions, hardware failover microbehavior, and compound distributed change interactions; these limits and their artifact evidence are documented and archived (see Disclosure and execution/transformation_manifest.json). Operational implications. For operational adoption, verify extension requirements: (1) broaden verifier semantics to vendor‑specific and multi‑change compound effects; (2) define human‑in‑loop escalation and rollback contracts for out‑of‑scope proposals; (3) conduct larger, higher‑hazard trials across multiple proposer models to measure practical impact. Reproducibility and audit. All raw outputs, provider calls, verifier traces and analysis scripts are archived with SHA‑256 hashes in the execution_manifest and analysis artifact list to enable deterministic replay. The minimal file set required to reproduce the confirmatory table and figure is enumerated in Methods and in the Disclosure. Limitations. Single‑model scope, canonical task bank, verifier coverage limits, low baseline failure prevalence, and sandbox abstraction vs vendor devices constrain generalization; we discuss them below and in the Disclosure.
sections.conclusion: A fully preregistered paired experiment (N=300) demonstrates that an LLM proposer (gpt‑5‑mini) gated by a deterministic network verifier plus one automated repair iteration repaired the single verifier‑detectable unsafe baseline proposal observed (task‑000165). Observed paired absolute reduction = 0.003333 (0.3333 percentage points); McNemar p = 1.00; bootstrap 95% CI = [0.00, 0.01]. The run validates reproducible GVR mechanics, deterministic acceptance traces, and archival auditability. Wider operational claims require larger experiments with higher baseline hazard rates, multiple proposer models, and expanded verifier coverage. All raw outputs, verifier traces, provider calls, and analysis scripts are archived for deterministic replay (execution_manifest and analysis artifacts cited in the Disclosure).

limitations: Single‑model limitation: experiments used a single proposer (gpt‑5‑mini); results do not establish multi‑model generality.
Canonical task bank: tasks were deterministic canonical templates (routing, ACL, BGP); production change distributions may differ materially and have higher baseline failure rates.

Verifier coverage: the deterministic verifier models a canonical subset (reachability regressions, ACL/policy flips, parse/semantic invalidity, mandated‑connectivity removals) but omits some vendor‑specific coupled behaviors and multi‑change interactions (verifier implementation and decision rules archived: execution/transformation_manifest.json SHA‑256: f3ac5460...).
Low baseline failure prevalence: only 1/300 baseline unsafe proposals were observed, limiting statistical power and widening uncertainty for modest absolute reductions.

Sandbox abstraction: the canonical sandbox is a model of device semantics for deterministic checking and is not a substitute for vendor device execution; production deployment requires extended validation on vendor devices and in live canary trials.
